name: Get Set for School: Readiness & Writing Pre-K Teacher's Guide (Learning Without Tears, 8th Edition)

layer1_philosophy.methodology: Handwriting Without Tears / Learning Without Tears developmental, multisensory letter formation (the publisher rebranded from Handwriting Without Tears to Learning Without Tears years ago; every page footer in this PDF reads Learning Without Tears, and the specific book is the Get Set for School Pre-K line's Readiness & Writing Teacher's Guide, not a standalone book titled Handwriting Without Tears)
principles: Multisensory readiness before paper: children build capital letters and a human figure (the guide calls it Mat Man) out of wooden pieces representing the basic strokes (a big line, a little line, a big curve, a little curve) so the letter shapes are learned by hand before they are ever written

Letters and numbers are grouped and taught by the family of strokes that forms them, not alphabetically or numerically. Capitals are grouped as Vertical and Horizontal letters, then Magic C letters (round, start like a C), then Big and Little Curves, then Diagonals. Lowercase letters regroup again into a same-as-capitals set, a Magic c set, a transition set, a set the guide calls Diver Letters (start high, dive below the baseline), and a final set

Capitals are taught before lowercase. The guide's own reasoning: capitals are one size, always start at the top, and use only straight lines and simple curves, which is developmentally easier than the two-story, ascender/descender shapes of lowercase letters

Every stroke of every letter and number is narrated aloud with the same small, consistent vocabulary (line, curve, big, little, up, down, across) while the parent models and the child copies stroke by stroke, so the same words always cue the same motion

A Wet-Dry-Try multisensory sequence on a small slate: wet a sponge and wipe the letter shape, dry it with a cloth, then trace it with chalk, practicing the same motion three sensory ways before the child ever picks up a pencil

A full developmental progression across the guide: body awareness and gross/fine motor play, then drawing and pre-writing stroke practice (lines, curves, basic shapes), then guided letter formation with a model to trace and copy, then independent writing. Number writing and early counting run in parallel using the same stroke-narration technique and a matching Starting Corner cue

Assessment is by developmental benchmark and teacher observation, not testing. Support and differentiation notes for English language learners are built into every single lesson, not bolted on separately

The guide is explicitly research-grounded: it closes with a bibliography of more than 60 sources spanning developmental psychology, early literacy research, and occupational therapy studies on pencil grip and prewriting skill development

knowledgeBankGaps.title: Handwriting Without Tears / Learning Without Tears Method
knowledgeBankGaps.summary: A developmental, multisensory approach to teaching letter and number formation. Letters are grouped and taught by shared stroke family (straight lines, Magic C curves, big/little curves, diagonals), not alphabetically. Capitals are taught before lowercase because they are simpler and more uniform. Every stroke is narrated with a small consistent verbal vocabulary (big line, little line, curve) while a parent models and the child copies. Readiness activities build body awareness and the same basic strokes with wooden pieces before any pencil work begins, and a wet-dry-try slate sequence rehearses each letter's motion three sensory ways before paper. Assessment is developmental benchmark and observation, not testing.

knowledgeBankGaps.title: Get Set for School Pre-K Readiness & Writing Teacher's Guide Format
knowledgeBankGaps.summary: A single Pre-K teacher's guide (8th edition, 2021, Learning Without Tears) organized into nine skill sections rather than numbered weeks: Readiness, Drawing, Alphabet Knowledge, Colors & Coloring, Pre-Writing, Writing Capital Letters (all 26), Counting & Numbers, Writing Lowercase Letters (all 26), and a Resources appendix (formation charts, an index, and the research bibliography). Each letter or number gets its own lesson page with a consistent template: a model to look at, guided trace-and-copy practice, a check step, an ELL support note, and a Look What We're Learning skills box (foundation skills, writing, sensory-motor, oral language, vocabulary). No day-by-day or week-by-week calendar is given; pacing is left to the teacher's judgment of the child's readiness. The guide is written for a classroom teacher as much as a homeschool parent (it references classroom routines, circle time, and a classroom environment throughout), which is a real product consideration for how Homa should adapt it for a one-child homeschool setting.

layer3_structure.cadence: Not stated as a weekly calendar anywhere in either PDF. Unlike a Charlotte Mason-style guide (e.g. the already-ingested Blossom & Root Level 0), this Pre-K teacher's guide is organized by developmental skill section, not by numbered week: Introduction, Readiness, Drawing, Alphabet Knowledge, Colors & Coloring, Pre-Writing, Writing Capital Letters, Counting & Numbers, Writing Lowercase Letters, then Resources. The guide explicitly leaves pacing to the teacher's judgment of the child's readiness rather than a fixed schedule

sessionLengthMinutes.note: Not stated. Unlike Blossom & Root's guides, which give explicit per-activity minute counts, the sampled pages of this guide describe activities as short and daily in general terms (e.g. one letter or one number per lesson) without printing a minutes figure. Recording an invented number here would not be honest; leaving this unknown rather than guessing

layer3_structure.weeklyTemplate: No week-by-week template exists in the source. Every letter and number lesson instead follows the same fixed page template regardless of which week it falls in: a model to Look and Learn from, a Trace and Copy practice step, a Check step, a Support/ELL note, and a Look What We're Learning skills box covering foundation skills, writing, sensory-motor, oral language, and vocabulary for that one letter or number. The guide's own suggested sequence is: Readiness (body awareness and wood-piece stroke play) before Drawing and Alphabet Knowledge, before Pre-Writing (stroke and shape tracing), before Writing Capital Letters (all 26, in stroke-family order), running alongside Counting & Numbers (counting, numeral recognition, and digit formation), before Writing Lowercase Letters (all 26, in a second stroke-family order)
layer3_structure.progressionModel: developmental-mastery, not spiral or fixed-linear: strokes and letters are sequenced from developmentally easier to harder (straight lines before curves before diagonals; capitals before lowercase) and the guide expects the teacher to judge readiness rather than advance on a calendar
layer3_structure.reviewRhythm: The Capital Letter Formation Chart, Lowercase Formation Chart, and Number Formation Chart in the Resources section function as ongoing quick-reference review tools rather than periodic tests. Development is tracked through stated Benchmarks (referenced repeatedly in the guide's own index) rather than scored assessments
layer3_structure.notes: This guide's own index lists 'classroom environment', 'classroom routines', and 'child development' as recurring topics, and the Readiness section repeatedly frames activities in terms of a group/classroom setting. This is a K-12-school-market teacher's guide (Learning Without Tears sells primarily into preschools and elementary schools) that a homeschool parent is using one-to-one, not a guide written for a single child at home. curriculum-writer should account for that: activities described for a classroom (turn-taking games, group circle time cues) need a light one-child adaptation, not a literal transcription.

activityTypes.description: A single capital letter's own lesson page: a large model letter with its verbal stroke cue underneath (for example, 'Big line down. Little line across the top.'), a row of trace boxes that fade from a solid model to a blank independent-write box, and a starting-point dot marking exactly where the first stroke begins. Letters appear in the guide's own stroke-family order (Vertical & Horizontal, then Magic C, then Big & Little Curves, then Diagonals), not alphabetical order.

suggestedRecipe.name: letter-number-formation-practice
suggestedRecipe.description: One letter or digit per page (or half-page): a bold model with a plain-language stroke cue, a formation box (single box for capitals/digits, a three-band ceiling/chair-rail/floor box for lowercase), 4-6 trace repetitions fading from full model to blank, and a starting dot. Groups by shared stroke family when the family's curriculum specifies one.

activityTypes.description: The same per-letter lesson template as the capitals, but every lowercase letter's box uses a three-band floor/chair-rail/ceiling line system (since lowercase letters are two-story: tall letters reach the ceiling, round letters stay in the middle band, descenders drop below the floor), and letters are grouped in a second, different stroke-family teaching order from the capitals.
activityTypes.notes: Same recipe as capital-letter-formation-practice above; the recipe's design patterns cover both the single-box (capital/digit) and three-band (lowercase) box geometry as two variants of one format, not two separate recipes.

activityTypes.description: A single digit (0-9) with a Number Formation Chart stroke cue and a Number Stories mnemonic (a short verbal story that makes the digit's shape memorable), trace boxes, and independent writing practice, using the same Starting Corner cue as the capital letters.
activityTypes.notes: Close but not exact: number-practice-page already gives a single-numeral trace section on a generic 3-line guide plus a ten-frame, number-word, and count-and-color section on the same page, which is a stronger multi-activity page than this source's simpler formation-only pages. It does not currently narrate the stroke with the letter-number-formation-practice recipe's plain-language cue style. Recording this as a low-urgency future design-pattern addition to number-practice-page rather than building a third, near-duplicate number recipe.

activityTypes.description: Straight-line, curved-line, and basic-shape tracing pages for children not yet ready for real letters, using the same box-and-fade-trace pattern as the letter pages but with no letter at all, just the stroke shape itself.
activityTypes.notes: Covered by the same new recipe as a simpler variant (a formation box with a stroke shape instead of a letter); no separate recipe needed.

activityTypes.description: A hands-on readiness activity: the child physically assembles a human figure (Mat Man) and, separately, individual capital letters out of wooden pieces shaped like the four basic strokes (big line, little line, big curve, little curve), before any pencil is picked up.
activityTypes.notes: This is a physical manipulative activity with real wooden (or paper-cutout) pieces, not a printable page; it sits outside what materials-studio produces, the same way the CM toddler-band guides in curriculum-writer.md note that some activities are real-world and not anything materials-studio would generate. No recipe gap to flag here on purpose.

activityTypes.description: A multisensory letter-tracing sequence on a small chalkboard slate: wet a small sponge and wipe the letter shape away, dry it with a cloth, then trace the letter in chalk, rehearsing the same motion three different sensory ways before it ever meets paper.
activityTypes.notes: Also a physical, non-printable activity (slate, sponge, chalk), out of scope for materials-studio the same way as wood-piece building above.

activityTypes.description: Alphabet Knowledge activities where the child matches a capital letter to its lowercase partner, or finds a target letter hiding among distractors.
Simple line-art pages the child colors while a parent names and reinforces color words, plus general fine-motor coloring-within-the-lines practice.
activityTypes.notes: coloring-page is a long-standing activity-formats.md entry generated on the image-direct path; it has no dedicated recipes/*.md file (like handwriting-practice and tracing-guide, it predates the recipe-file system), but it is well-established and simple enough that authoring a new recipe file for it would be duplicate work, not a genuine gap.

notes: Real page counts, verified directly rather than assumed from the filenames: hwt-pt1.pdf is 120 PDF pages (a CamScanner phone scan of physical book spreads, some early pages scanned two or three times by accident) covering physical book pages 1 through 229; hwt-pt2.pdf is 24 PDF pages covering physical book pages 230 through the end of the book (roughly page 276, including the blank Notes pages at the very back). The two PDFs are confirmed to be ONE continuous book split across two Slack uploads, not two different books, grade levels, or editions: pt2's very first lesson page (capital/lowercase E) picks up exactly where pt1's last lesson page (capital/lowercase I) leaves off, mid-way through the same 'Transition Group' of the guide's own Lowercase Teaching Order, and every page in both files carries the identical footer ('Readiness & Writing PreK Teacher's Guide' / '(c) 2021 Learning Without Tears'). The book itself is titled 'Get Set for School (r) by Learning Without Tears: Readiness & Writing Pre-K Teacher's Guide', 8th edition, copyright 2021 Learning Without Tears, the modern rebrand of the company Aless knows as Handwriting Without Tears; this is that company's current Pre-K handwriting-and-readiness volume, not a book with 'Handwriting Without Tears' literally on its cover. It is a school-market teacher's guide (references classroom routines and circle time throughout) rather than a homeschool-authored curriculum, which is worth keeping in mind anywhere Homa adapts its activities for a single child at home. Sampling covered the front matter and table of contents (pt1 pages 1-10), the Readiness section including Wood Piece Play, Mat Man, and pencil-grip guidance (pt1 pages 21-30), the Pre-Writing-to-Capital-Letters transition and the Developmental Teaching stroke-family order (pt1 pages 61-70), the Counting & Numbers section (pt1 pages 91-100), the end of Writing Capital Letters into the start of Writing Lowercase Letters (pt1 pages 111-120), the remainder of Writing Lowercase Letters through the alphabet's end (pt2 pages 1-8), and the Resources section: Help Me Write My Name, the full index, the References bibliography, and the Capital/Lowercase/Number Formation Charts (pt2 pages 17-24). This is representative sampling across the full breadth of both files as instructed, not a page-by-page read of all 144 combined PDF pages. Copyrighted page images and exact proprietary wording (letter mnemonics, Number Stories text, trademarked terms like Mat Man and Wet-Dry-Try) were used only for this session's own analysis and are described here in Homa's own words, never reproduced verbatim into any product file; the new letter-number-formation-practice recipe describes a generic box-and-stroke-cue pedagogy pattern in Homa's own voice, not a copy of this publisher's specific letters, mnemonics, or illustrations.
